bank.title: Methodist Central Hall
bank.caption: Positioned directly across the street from Westminster Abbey, there's a touch of irony here. I originally didn't like this shot much, but it came out nice after some edits to bring out the texture of the building and the color of the sky.

clockcompound.title: Well Court [1]
clockcompound.caption: In Dean Village, along the Water of Leith Walkway.

clocktower.title: Well Court, Dean Village [2]
clocktower.caption: Still in Dean Village, and still along the Water of Leith Walkway.

courtyard.title: Westminster Abbey Courtyard
courtyard.caption: Westminster Abbey's main cloister and courtyard.

crumble.title: St Anthony's Chapel
crumble.caption: Found on a side-path about a quarter of the way up the hike to the top of Arthur's Seat.

nook.title: Shell Grotto
nook.caption: Found at the Queen Mother’s Memorial Garden in the Royal Botanic Garden in Edinburgh. Felt like something you'd find on your Tumblr feed circa 2009.

power.title: Battersea Power Station
power.caption: The hotel I stayed at in London was right across the street. I wouldn't recommend the hotel, but I would recommend stopping by the power station if you like architecture. Not really worth going inside since its a pretty standard mall these days, though.

wes.title: The Botanic Cottage
wes.caption: A quaint cottage found in the Royal Botanic Garden in Edinburgh. I didn't get the shot quite right, needing to take it lower; but, you live and you learn.

westminster.title: Westminster Abbey North Door
westminster.caption: The tourist entrance to Westminster Abbey. The main one is reserved for folks coming to a service.

disappointment.title: Historia and Eloquence
disappointment.caption: The overall monument is to William Ewart Gladstone, a prominent Scottish statesmen. Surrounding the state are virtues, 2 of which are pictured here. As far as I could tell, Eloquence is the one with the cone over their head. If whoever placed it knew that, I hope they recognize their comedic genius.

horseman.title: The Royal Scots Greys Monument
horseman.caption: A memorial to the Royal Scots Greys cavalry regiment, commemorating those who fought and died in the Second Boer War and other conflicts.

kid.title: Robert Fergusson
kid.caption:
A prominent Scottish poet in the era of the Scottish Enlightenment. An excerpt from one of his most famous works on material vs. intellectual wealth, [Braid Claith](https://www.scottishpoetrylibrary.org.uk/poem/braid-claith/):

Ye wha are fain to hae your name
    Wrote in the bonny book of fame,
    Let merit nae pretension claim
        To laurel'd wreath,
    But hap ye weel, baith back and wame,
        In gude Braid Claith.

poli.title: Adam Smith
poli.caption: Statue to Adam Smith, a Scottish economist, philosopher, and the author of Wealth of Nations. I was surprised by the number of notable Scottish philosophers, and Edinburgh seemed to take significant pride in their country's intellectual history. Edinburgh is sometimes referred to as "the Athens of the North" because of this, and even tried to build their own full-scale replica of the Parthenon as a national monument. If you've ever seen it, you'll know to put emphasis on "tried".

saint.title: Sir Walter Scott
saint.caption: Sir Walter Scott, a Scottish author, is the subject of the Scott Monument in Edinburgh.

seated.title: James Clerk Maxwell
seated.caption: One of history's most influential physicists. I hear he had an [(electro)magnetic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Dynamical_Theory_of_the_Electromagnetic_Field) personality.

swag.title: James Braidwood
swag.caption: Allegedly, James Braidwood was the creator of the world's first municipal Fire Department.

cannons.title: Tower of London Battlement Sign
cannons.caption: Taken near the entrance of a tower along the battlements surrounding the property.

castle.title: Edinburgh Coat of Arms
castle.caption: I believe this is the Edinburgh Coat of Arms, engraved on an old police box. None of the police boxes in Edinburgh are actually in use by the force these days, with most being leased to micro cafes and such. This one had seen better days, and didn't seem to see any use.

crest.title: Scottish Achievement
crest.caption: Scottish coat of arms with heraldic achievement, at Castle Edinburgh.

crunch.title: Bronze 24-Pounder Cannon Heraldry
crunch.caption: Likely a depiction of Satan, being consumed by 2 dragons. Ouch.

dog.title: Bronze 24-Pounder Cannon Maltese Quoin
dog.caption: The quoin used to support the barrel of this cannon is in the shape of a Maltese dog, a nod to its commissioners: the Order of St John (otherwise known as the Order of Malta).

dragon.title: Westminster Abbey Dragon
dragon.caption: Likely depicts the dragon St. George is fabled to have slain.

fence.title: Fence [1]
fence.caption: Note much to say here, but I liked the ironwork.

grate.title: Bloody Mackenzie's Mausoleum
grate.caption: I didn't know what I was photographing until later, but this is a grate on the doors to one of the most famous graves in Greyfriar's Kirkyard: [Bloody Mackenzie's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Mackenzie_of_Rosehaugh) Mausoleum. He was a Scottish lawyer and prominent figure of the [Covenanters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Covenanters) that earned the name by being one of the its ruthless prosecutors.

pulpit.title: Preaching Tent
pulpit.caption: A preaching tent at the National Museum of Scotland. I liked the way the lighting was setup in the exhibit, and the texture of the wood. Outdoor services were particular popular in Scotland following the [Disruption of 1843](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disruption_of_1843), where ministers across the country broke away from the Church of Scotland. The Scots certainly were (are?) quite a cantankerous bunch.

swords.title: Fence [2]
swords.caption: Another fence with some nice ironwork, this one featuring some sort of stylized fleur-de-lis points.

unicorn.title: Unicorn Relief at the King's Gallery
unicorn.caption: Found on the door to the King's Gallery at the Palace of Holyroodhouse. Positioned across from the British Lion, the much less interesting National mascot of the UK countries.

wheel.title: Bronze 24-Pounder Cannon Wheel
wheel.caption: Surely the cost of these wheels would have made even [Tim Cook blush](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mBHY_Qaw5AI).

apostles.title: The Holy Ghost
apostles.caption: Likely a depiction of [Acts 2:4](https://www.biblegateway.com/verse/en/Acts%202%3A4), where a group was filled with the Holy Spirit and began to speak in tongues.

demure.title: Stained Glass
demure.caption: I don't remember exactly where this was; maybe somewhere in St John's Chapel? Definitely somewhere at the Tower of London.

flood.title: The Flood
flood.caption: I'm not certain what is being depicted here, but there's definitely a religious figure guiding (or punishing?) a group of sailors. Some of the stained glass in Westminster Abbey is actually [quite modern](https://www.westminster-abbey.org/history/explore-our-history/stained-glass), and I'd guess this falls into that category based on the richness of the cool colors, particularly the deep blues and purples.

mixed.title: The Battle of Britain Memorial Window
mixed.caption: This is a fairly modern (1947) installment in the [RAF Chapel](https://www.westminster-abbey.org/history/explore-our-history/raf-chapel) of Westminster Abbey. Something I found interesting in the UK was that stained glass memorializing those lost in battle, particularly in the World Wars, were fairly common (both in Scotland and England); I had previously only seen religious imagery depicted on holy grounds.

renala.title: Sir Charles and Sir John Wolfe Barry
renala.caption: There's something odd about seeing a king and a civil engineer enshrined in the [nave](https://www.westminster-abbey.org/abbey-commemorations/commemorations/sir-charles-and-sir-john-wolfe-barry) of Westminster Abbey. Sir John Wolfe Barry designed multiple prominent bridges in the London area, including Blackfriars Bridge.

strategem.title: Major-General Andrew Gilbert Wauchope
strategem.caption: Taken at St Giles' Cathedral in Edinburgh, in memory of a major-general who died in the Battle of Magersfontein in the Second Boer War. One of the more interesting pieces of Scottish history I learned while in Edinburgh is that much of England's military victories were paid for in Scottish blood. Its strange to see a monument to such an unjust conflict in a place like this.

zealot.title: Guardian of Scotland
zealot.caption: This glass is from the oldest building on the Castle Edinburgh grounds: [St Margaret's Chapel](https://www.edinburghcastle.scot/see-and-do/highlights/st-margarets-chapel/). It depicts Sir William Wallace, one of the main leaders during the First War of Scottish Independence.

1.title: James Harlay Monument
1.caption: This one was tough to trace down, but it appears to be the grave of [James Harlay](https://fogk.org/2025/08/10/the-east-wall/). I can't find much about him, other than that he was "Keeper of His Majesties Privy Seal", which sounds... nevermind.

2.title: Borthwick Monument
2.caption: The most striking thing to me about the monuments and murals in Greyfriars Kirkyard was that so few seemed to depict religious imagery, instead showing memento mori symbols. Supposedly there are potentially hundreds or thousands of bodies on the grounds despite there being only 750 grave markers; so it makes sense that this would have started to feel like a Godless place at some point. This particular mural was in memory of James Borthwick, a famed surgeon, hence the depiction of various surgical instruments.

booba.title: Displaced Finial
booba.caption: I believe this is a stone finial that would normally be atop some sort of gate or decorative pillar, but has broken off. The design may be of an acorn, which is representative of the cycle of rebirth.

ded.title: Momento Mori Stone
ded.caption: This headstone was off to the side, with no notable accompanying plaque or text. Since the kirkyard is thought to contain tens to hundreds of thousands of bodies, I took this as a marker to the less distinguished residents.

grave.title: George Heriot Monument
grave.caption:
Although it can't really be deciphered now, the [inscription once read](https://www.findagrave.com/memorial/85276703/george-heriot):

Passenger, who art wise, hence know whence you are,
what you are, and what you are to be,
Life, gate of death; Death, gate of life to me,
Sole death of death gives life eternally.
Therefore, whoever breathe draws from the air,
While live thou may'st, thyself for death prepare.

headless.title: This I'll Defend
headless.caption: This is the heraldic coat of arms of [Clan Macfarlane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clan_MacFarlane), whose motto was "this I'll defend". The banner paired with the coat of arms' headless guardians is quite a statement on the inevitability of death and the futility of earthly squabbles.

heads.title: John Mylne III Memorial
heads.caption: It took some digging, but I believe this is the grave of [John Mylne III](https://www.findagrave.com/memorial/75232661/john-mylne), Master Mason to the Crown of Scotland. I also believe these faces are some variation of [Green Men](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Man), foliaged figures meant to represent rebirth. Their somewhat grotesque appearance is likely also to ward off evil spirits from the burial grounds.

hut.title: St. George's Well
hut.caption: It's a shame to see something nearly as old as the United States vandalized, but the water from this well's spring is [notoriously foul tasting](https://www.megalithic.co.uk/article.php?sid=15325), so I guess its fitting that the exterior has been made to match.

spooy.title: The Foulis Memorial
spooy.caption: A [monument](https://fogk.org/2025/07/11/the-foulis-memorial/) to the Laird of Ravelston and his wife, constructed by his son George Foulis of Ravelston.

bench.title: Bench
bench.caption: A bench along the Water of Leith Walkway.

bird.title: Arthur's Roost
bird.caption: A bird seen near the ruins of St Anthony's Chapel on the way to the top of Arthur's Seat.

buttercup.title: St. John's Wort
buttercup.caption: At least I'm pretty sure this is some variant of St. John's Wart ([hypericum 'hidcote'](https://data.rbge.org.uk/search/livingcollection/?eti=Hypericum&cfg=livcol.cfg&acc_num=&acc_num_qual=&barcode=)). Its a surprisingly hardy plant, and depending on where it grows it has slightly different characteristics. The petals of these flowers are fairly broad, for example.

fairies.title: Mystic Water
fairies.caption: A water feature at the Royal Botanic Garden in Edinburgh.

lily.title: Water Lily
lily.caption: A lone water lily in one of the ponds at the Royal Botanic Garden in Edinburgh.

pinky.title: Codlins & Cream
pinky.caption: Otherwise known as great willowherb ([epilobium hirsutum](https://data.rbge.org.uk/search/livingcollection/?eti=Epilobium+hirsutum&cfg=livcol.cfg&acc_num=&acc_num_qual=&barcode=)), but who'd use that name when "codlins and cream" is an option.

yellowflowers.title: Ragwort
yellowflowers.caption: This is some kind of ragwort, which are members of the Daisy family. Possibly redstem ragwort ([senecio achilleifolius](https://data.rbge.org.uk/search/livingcollection/?eti=Senecio&cfg=livcol.cfg&acc_num=&acc_num_qual=&barcode=))? Its tough to tell.
